site.name: meadowos
site.summary: meadowos-clone Fictional self-hosted home OS "MeadowOS" marketing site (magazine / zine-style long-scroll narrative). Pages | File | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `index.html` | Single-page long scroll: thin top nav + progress bar; hero with hand-drawn SVG house and flower illustration; five chapters (Roman numerals I–V) of magazine-prose with pull quotes and chapter illustrations; mid-page "Garden" 6-card plant-app grid (Nextfile / Bramble / Cottage / Smithy / Hearth / Postcard); reviewer quotes; terminal-style .iso download block + platform pills + minimum / recommended specs; six numbered manifesto items; dark footer | | `styles.css` | Brand color #2F5233 dark green, accent terracotta + wheat yellow, cream paper background; Crimson Pro serif + Inter; cards with slight rotate + paper-shadow; responsive | | `script.js` | Top scroll progress bar; smooth anchor scrolling; clicking "Download .iso" triggers a fake download-progress modal (increments to 100% then shows SHA256 verification passed) |

run_plan.goal: Validate the UX of the MeadowOS single-page marketing site, focusing on narrative flow, interactive download simulation, and mobile responsiveness.
run_plan.summary: The run will traverse the long-scroll landing page using both top navigation anchors and manual scrolling to verify content hierarchy. It will trigger the 'Download .iso' button to validate the fake progress modal and SHA256 verification state. Finally, it will switch to a mobile viewport to audit the reported small tap targets and layout stability.
assumptions: The site is a Single Page Application (SPA) style long-scroll; all 'pages' (Story, Garden, Docs) are sections within index.html.
The 'Download' interaction is a client-side simulation (fake progress bar) as described in the prescan, not a real file transfer.
The 'Garden' section contains static informational cards for apps (Nextfile, Bramble, etc.) rather than live application interfaces.
risk_hotspots: Download Modal: Verify the progress bar increments smoothly and the final 'SHA256 verification passed' state renders correctly.
Mobile Navigation: The prescan flagged multiple nav links (<44px height); verify if they are clickable or obscured by touch targets on mobile.
Scroll Progress Bar: Ensure the top indicator accurately reflects scroll depth through the five chapters.

phases.objective: Verify smooth scrolling behavior and content visibility for the primary narrative sections.
key_checks: Click 'Story', 'Garden', 'Docs', and 'Get the .iso' nav links to test anchor jumping.

exit_criteria: All nav anchors successfully scroll to their respective sections.

phases.title: Interactive Download Flow
phases.objective: Test the primary conversion action and its feedback loop.
key_checks: Locate and click the 'Download · meadowos-0.7.iso' button.
Observe the modal appearance and progress bar animation (0% to 100%).
Confirm the final state displays 'SHA256 verification passed'.
Close the modal and verify the background page remains interactive.

phases.title: Garden App Grid Inspection
phases.objective: Review the presentation of the ecosystem apps within the 'Garden' section.
key_checks: Inspect the 6-card grid (Nextfile, Bramble, Cottage, Smithy, Hearth, Postcard).
Check for hover states on cards (rotation/shadow effects mentioned in CSS).
Verify card text is readable and aligned.
exit_criteria: All 6 app cards are visible and styled correctly.

phases.title: Mobile Viewport & Accessibility Audit
phases.objective: Address prescan warnings regarding small tap targets and layout on narrow screens.
key_checks: Switch viewport to mobile (e.g., iPhone SE or Pixel 5 dimensions).
Attempt to tap 'Story', 'Garden', and 'Docs' links; note if they are difficult to hit.
Check if the hamburger menu (if present) or nav collapses gracefully.
Verify the 'Download' button is full-width or easily tappable.
Check text readability for the long-form prose on small screens.
exit_criteria: Navigation is usable despite small target warnings.
Content reflows correctly without horizontal scroll.
Download CTA is prominent and accessible.

coverage_targets.pages: 100% of index.html sections (Hero, Story Ch I-V, Garden, Download, Footer)
coverage_targets.features: Nav anchors, Scroll progress bar, Download modal simulation, Card hover states

notes: Since this is a local file system path, network errors are not expected, but console JS errors should be monitored during the modal interaction.
Pay attention to the 'Manifesto' section near the footer to ensure the numbered list formats correctly on mobile.

prescan_summary.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
prescan_summary.visible_text_excerpt: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Story Garden Docs Get the .iso Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or t

observation.title: MeadowOS — Bring your data home
observation.visible_text: MeadowOS Read time · ~6 min Plant your data in a meadow. A small, friendly operating system for your own server. Run the apps you love. Tend them like a garden. A small home for your photos, your notes, your mail, your files. Not in someone else's cloud. I. The Cloud is Someone Else's House. You moved into a place you don't own. You hung your photographs on rented walls. The landlord raised the rent — three times last year. They walked into your bedroom and rearranged the furniture. They told you when guests could visit and which windows you could open. When you complained, they sent you a 47-page Terms of Service in a font designed to discourage you from reading it. This is the situation we are in. Our memories live on disks that we cannot point to on a map. Our notes are subject to deprecations. Our address books vanish in mergers. We accept it because the alternative — running a server — is presented as a thing for systems administrators in basements, or for people who genuinely enjoy reading journalctl for sport. "You moved into a place you don't own." We don't think it has to be that way. We think most people, given a small, friendly tool, can keep a server alive for the same effort it takes to keep a houseplant alive. So we built one. your house II. A Patch of Land. What you need is small. A cheap computer the size of a paperback novel, a power cable, a router, and an afternoon. A Raspberry Pi 5, perhaps. A retired ThinkPad you couldn't bear to throw out. An old Mac mini your cousin gave you. Any of these will hold more data than you will accumulate in a lifetime. MeadowOS turns that small machine into a quiet, dependable place to put your things. It comes as a single 1.2 GB .iso. You write it to a USB stick. You boot the computer. You walk through five questions. You're done. It is, on purpose, almost boring. "It is, on purpose, almost boring." $ meadow init III. What Grows Here. You don't install software on MeadowOS so much as you plant it. Each app is a tidy package — a single icon, a single description, a single "Plant" button. You water it occasionally. You weed out the ones you don't use. There are, at the time of this writing, about forty available. Below: the most popular six. Each one replaces something you currently rent from a company that does not know your name. Nextfile Your files. Sync between devices. End-to-end encrypted on the wire. ~12MB on disk. replaces · Dropbox Bramble RSS reader. Subscribe to anything. Read offline. No tracking pixels survive the moat. replaces · Feedly Cottage Photos. Albums. Faces (locally — never uploaded). Auto-import from your phone over Wi-Fi. replaces · iCloud Photos Smithy Self-hosted git. Pull requests, issues, CI. A lighter, friendlier Gitea. replaces · GitHub (for personal repos) Hearth Notes & journals. Markdown. Daily-page habit. Searchable from anywhere on your meadow. replaces · Notion (the small bits) Postcard Mail. IMAP+SMTP+spam handled. Bring your own domain — we'll guide you through the DNS. replaces · Gmail IV. The Tools in the Shed. The console is honest. There's a dashboard that shows you what's running, what's eating disk, what's running hot. There's an automatic backup that mirrors a snapshot to a second drive every night at 3 a.m., and to an off-site location of your choosing every Sunday. Restore is a single button. We tested it. We tested it the way we'd want it tested. When something breaks — and it will, occasionally; this is a computer — the failure is legible. Logs in plain English. A "what changed today" timeline. A red button that says "Roll back the last update," which actually rolls back the last update. "It feels less like an OS and more like a place." — Maren Ostrowski, The Quiet Wire V. Tend, Don't Manage. MeadowOS is not for the data center. It is not multi-tenant. It does not federate across regions. It will not survive the apocalypse and it will not keep your business compliant with HIPAA. It is for one or two or four people who would lik
